A B S T R A C T
We introduce HPR-GenRM, a hierarchical process-level generative reward model for robust large 
language model (LLM) alignment in offline reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) 
settings, unifying long-horizon reasoning with explicit step-by-step verification through a three-
tier architecture. Training on 25K hierarchically-annotated instances from HelpSteer2, MATH, 
and CodeContests, our Llama-3-8B-based model achieves 82.3% accuracy on RM-Bench (7.2% 
improvement over state-of-the-art), 89.1% step accuracy on MATH-500 with error localization 
F1 of 0.83, and 61% relative reduction in undetected adversarial attacks. Integration into 
RLHF yields 58.3% win rate on AlpacaEval2 (11.1% gain) while reducing policy-level reward 
hacking from 15% to 5%. This work presents hierarchical process-level reasoning as an effective 
approach for interpretable reward modeling within offline reward labeling and quality-sensitive 
alignment settings.

sections.heading: Related
sections.text: work Reward modeling for RLHF traditionally relies on the Bradley–Terry framework ( Christiano et al. , 2017 ; Zhang et al. , 2024 ), where pairwise preference data trains discriminative models to predict scalar rewards. Subsequent work scaled these to large language models ( Guo et al. , 2025 ; Stiennon et al. , 2020 ), yet core limitations persist: large preference datasets are required, and policies exploit model weaknesses through reward hacking ( Gao et al. , 2023 ; Rafailov et al. , 2024 ). Even strong models remain brittle under distribution shift ( J. Hong et al. , 2025 ), and ensemble mitigation ( Coste et al. , 2023 ) multiplies cost without resolving the root issue: scalar predictions carry no intermediate reasoning for verification. GenRMs produce natural language rationales rather than scalar scores, improving data efficiency and interpretability ( Dong et al. , 2023 ; Mahan et al. , 2024 ; Wang et al. , 2024 ). DeepSeek-GRM ( Liu et al. , 2025 ) shows that self-principled critique tuning with 32× sampling at 27B surpasses a 671B greedy baseline. Yet most GenRMs use shallow reasoning chains (100–300 tokens), which limits evaluation of tasks that require deep contextual understanding ( He et al. , 2025 ; Khalid et al. , 2025 ). Their unstructured nature also prevents step-level error localization. Process reward models assess intermediate reasoning steps rather than only final outcomes ( Uesato et al. , 2022 ). Lightman et al. ( 2023 ) showed step-level annotations improve sample efficiency in mathematical reasoning. GenPRM ( Zhao et al. , 2025 ) extends this to generative settings via chain-of-thought rationales and code verification, which enables test-time scaling through majority voting. ThinkPRM ( Khalifa et al. , 2025 ) pairs long chain-of-thought with process-level labels at low annotation cost. Both, however, assess each step with limited prior context and provide no architecture integrating global reasoning with step-level verification. Think-RM ( I. Hong et al. , 2025 ) introduces long-horizon reasoning (1000–3000 tokens) with self-reflection and hypothetical exploration. It selects the longest correct path from multiple samples and refines via group relative policy optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al. , 2024 ). Deeper reasoning per instance outperforms multiple shallow attempts on complex tasks. Nevertheless, Think-RM’s free-form output lacks explicit step boundaries and correctness labels, which prevents error localization and reduces robustness to adversarial manipulation. Generative reasoning, process verification, and long-horizon thinking each address one dimension of the problem while leaving complementary gaps: GenRMs lack step-level feedback, process RMs lack global context, and Think-RM lacks structured verification. Bridging all three requires a hierarchical design informed by inference-time scaling and alignment research, then tested directly in reward-modeling experiments. Ellis-Mohr et al. ( 2025 ) formalize inference-time scaling through DS3 and show that deeper reasoning per instance can substitute for training-time data scaling. Brown et al. ( 2024 ) validate this: 256 samples from a smaller model match a 4× larger model. Both focus on breadth scaling; neither addresses hierarchical structured verification for generative reward models. We carry the DS3 perspective into the hierarchical setting, treating depth and verification granularity as architectural choices that shape sample efficiency and adversarial robustness. Qi et al. ( 2024 ) show that safety alignment concentrates on the first few tokens, a ‘‘shallow alignment’’ bypassable by prefilling, adversarial suffixes, and fine-tuning attacks. Per-token KL (Kullback–Leibler divergence) analysis confirms later tokens remain largely unaligned ( Fehlauer et al. , 2025 ). Policies also exploit structural weaknesses in reward models during optimization ( Gao et al. , 2023 ; Skalse et al. , 2022 ), and ensemble mitigation ( Coste et al. , 2023 )

sections.heading: Objectives
sections.text: Building on the limitations identified in existing reward modeling approaches, this research pursues four objectives. First, we propose a hierarchical architecture that unifies long-horizon reasoning with explicit process-level verification to enable both deep contextual understanding and fine-grained error localization within a single framework. Second, we provide supporting structural analyses that motivate the choices of hierarchy depth, verification granularity, and adaptive depth allocation, and we report where the corresponding empirical patterns appear or weaken. Third, we present an effective training framework that combines hierarchical data generation, multi-objective supervised fine-tuning, and curriculum reinforcement learning to optimize verification at multiple granularities. Fourth, we validate the proposed approach through experiments that demonstrate improvements in preference accuracy, step-level verification, adversarial robustness, and downstream RLHF performance. sections.heading: Design
sections.text: rationale Three structural analyses in Appendix motivate the architectural choices that distinguish HPR-GenRM from single-tier baselines. The first analysis examines how hierarchical decomposition affects sample complexity. Since later tiers operate on increasingly compressed representations, the effective hypothesis class becomes smaller; this provides a rationale for the sample-efficiency pattern observed under distribution shift. The second analysis treats reward hacking as the joint failure of 𝐾 step-level verification checkpoints supported by 𝐷 tokens of internal reasoning. With the stated modeling assumptions, the idealized failure probability decreases as the product 𝐾 ⋅ 𝐷 grows. This reflects the design intuition that alignment signals should be distributed throughout generation rather than concentrated in a single outcome-level score. The third analysis considers how to spend a fixed token budget across instances of varying difficulty. It gives more depth to high-uncertainty instances and less depth to easier instances. Each analysis rests on simplifying assumptions stated alongside its theorem in the appendix. Section 7.11 then reports where these qualitative patterns appear in the experiments and where the idealized forms overstate the empirical effect. 6.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: 8.1. Architectural implications The structural analyses in Appendix motivate HPR-GenRM through two architectural properties. Composing tiers over pro- gressively compressed representations can limit the effective hypothesis class, which aligns with HPR-GenRM’s sample-efficiency advantage in Section 7.11 . Distributing alignment signal across 𝐾 ⋅ 𝐷 verification checkpoints makes adversarial inputs harder to construct, which aligns with the monotone-in- 𝐾 ⋅ 𝐷 detection curve. Section 7.11 also identifies where the idealized trends weaken: a sub-linear shift exponent ( 𝜂 ≈0 . 56 ) and mild positive step-failure correlation ( 𝜌 ≈0 . 12 ) reduce the empirical effect relative to the simplified analyses. The adaptive-depth rule adds a budget-allocation rationale whose sublinear shape is reflected in the empirical Pareto curve ( Fig. 5 ). 8.2. Practical implications HPR-GenRM has practical implications for offline and batch RLHF deployment. The interpretable step-level outputs let practi- tioners examine which specific steps failed when HPR-GenRM assigns a low reward, instead of treating the model as a black box. The 67% reduction in reward hacking (15% to 5%) addresses a deployment concern that single-tier rewards miss: hierarchical verification exposes shallow manipulation that produces high reward scores from low-quality outputs. The adaptive depth module trades inference cost for accuracy, with shallow reasoning on easy instances and deep verification on hard ones. The intended deployment scenarios are offline reward labeling and batch RLHF, where per-query inference time of several seconds can be amortized across batched scoring, and quality-sensitive alignment settings where step-level interpretability supports human oversight. Real-time use cases such as real-time chat moderation or sub-second content filtering fall outside the design envelope of the current 8B-scale system and would require distillation or architectural simplification (Section 9 ). 8.3. Comparison with existing approaches HPR-GenRM differs from existing approaches along two axes: reasoning depth and verification structure. It generates inter- pretable reasoning traces that BT models ( Christiano et al. , 2017 ) lack, and uses long-horizon reasoning (1000–2000 tokens) where shallow GenRMs ( Liu et al. , 2025 ; Mahan et al. , 2024 ) use 100–300, which yields a 7.2% RM-Bench improvement. Against GenPRM ( Zhao et al. , 2025 ), the extended internal reasoning before step-level verification means each step is assessed within the full trajectory; this accounts for the 10.9% step accuracy gain (89.1% vs. 78.2%). Against Think-RM ( I. Hong et al. , 2025 ), the explicit step boundaries and correctness labels enable error localization (F1 0.83 vs. 0.58) and actionable feedback for policy improvement. To understand the remaining 17.7% RM-Bench errors, we manually inspect 50 random failure cases. Three patterns dominate: (1) subtle multi-step errors (42%): both responses present plausible reasoning chains that differ in a single intermediate step, and Tier 3 cannot disambiguate near-equal step-correctness profiles; (2) domain-knowledge limits (34%): instances that need specialized knowledge (e.g., advanced physics, legal reasoning) the base model lacks; (3) cascading reasoning errors (24%): an incorrect Tier 1 initial hypothesis propagates through Tier 2 verification. Category (3) maps to the correlated-failure limitation (Section 9 ): a flawed Tier 1 hypothesis means downstream verification inherits the error. (1) and (3) likely require stronger base models or explicit cross-tier consistency checks; (2) may benefit from retrieval-augmented generation in Tier 1. sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Inference cost is the main limitation: 2100 tokens per query (8.4 s on 4 × RTX 4090) versus 1520 tokens (6.1 s) for Think-RM and 1.8 s for BT RM, a 38% overhead. Adaptive depth allocation cuts the average to 1820 tokens (7.3 s) with minimal accuracy loss, but the cost remains nontrivial for high-frequency deployments and impractical at 70B+ scale without distillation or architectural simplification. In its current form, HPR-GenRM should therefore be viewed as an offline reward-labeling and batch-RLHF method rather than a real-time reward scorer. Training requires hierarchical annotations (reasoning traces, step-level labels, step explanations), and quality filtering retains only 50%–60% of instances, which limits data efficiency. The verifier step depends on frontier-model APIs (GPT-4o or DeepSeek-R1) and creates a practical barrier for resource-limited groups; self-verification or lightweight discriminative verifiers could reduce this dependency. For such groups, Table 7 suggests a trade-off: the SFT-only variant omits hierarchical RL and still reaches 78.5% on RM-Bench (above all baselines), and the annotation pipeline can run on open-weight reasoning models such as QwQ-32B-Preview or DeepSeek-R1 in place of proprietary APIs, at much lower data-generation cost. The audit in Section 7.10 characterizes the residual noise as a ∼10% per-step error floor on a 1500 -instance stratified sample; this covers ∼6% of the 25K training corpus, and an exhaustive audit of the full pipeline remains future work. Our evaluation focuses on reasoning-intensive tasks (mathematical problem-solving, code understanding, preference compari- son); the benefits of hierarchical verification may diminish for tasks without multi-step reasoning, such as toxicity classification or short-form queries. The RLHF experiment uses 1000 PPO steps and provides evidence of short-term effectiveness, but it does not conclusively demonstrate long-term stability; extended training experiments are left for future work. The cross-model evidence (Section 7.12 ) is confined to four open-weight instruction-tuned base models in the 7–9B parameter band. Behavior at substantially larger scales ( ≥ 13B and especially ≥ 70B), at closed-weight families such as GPT-4 and Claude where the pipeline cannot be applied without API-level fine-tuning access, and under substantially different RLHF recipes (on-policy DPO, multi-turn dialog alignment, constitutional-AI critique loops) is not tested by the present experiments and is not claimed. The three-tier architecture introduces additional hyperparameters (five loss weights 𝛼 1 – 5 , three KL penalties 𝛽 step/traj/pref , depth bounds, filter thresholds) relative to single-tier baselines, which increases development complexity and may require extra tuning for new domains. The robustness analysis in Appendix A.2 assumes conditional independence of step verification failures; in practice, shared upstream reasoning errors cause correlated failures that weaken the idealized bound. The empirical 𝐾 ⋅ 𝐷 curve ( Fig. 6(b) ) is consistent with this limitation: gains under stronger Best-of-500 attacks show diminishing returns. Tighter analyses that account for cross-step correlation remain an open problem. Across 3 random seeds, RM-Bench variance is < 0 . 5% and MATH-500 step variance < 0 . 8% , which confirms stable training. AlpacaEval2 win-rate variance is largest (SD = 1 . 2% ), consistent with the known sensitivity of GPT-4 judging to prompt phrasing. 10.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: and future work We propose HPR-GenRM, a hierarchical process-level generative reward model for accurate, robust, and interpretable RLHF. The architecture unifies long-horizon reasoning with step-by-step verification through three tiers: extended internal reasoning, step decomposition with correctness labels, and integrated final preference judgment. The architectural choices are motivated by three structural analyses ( Appendix ) covering sample efficiency under distribution shift, robustness against reward hacking, and budget-aware depth allocation; Section 7.11 reports where the corresponding empirical patterns appear and where the idealized forms overstate the effect. On the empirical side, HPR-GenRM reaches 82.3% on RM-Bench ( +7 . 2 over Think-RM), 89.1% step accuracy on MATH-500 (error localization F1 = 0 . 83 ), and 58.3% AlpacaEval2 win rate when integrated into RLHF; policy-level reward hacking falls from 15% to 5% (67% relative reduction). These gains rest on standard benchmarks with human ground-truth labels and are therefore independent of the annotation verifier used during training. Ablation isolates Tier 2 (process verification) as the primary driver at +5 . 9 % on RM-Bench, above the RL training stage ( +3 . 8 %) and Tier 3 integration ( +2 . 2 %). Each tier addresses a specific limitation: Tier 1 supplies global context (10.9% step accuracy gain over GenPRM’s shallow per-step approach), Tier 2 adds step boundaries and correctness labels (the +5 . 9 % ablation gain and F1 = 0 . 83 ), and Tier 3 reconciles conflicting evidence sources (ECE = 0 . 058 ). The intended deployment envelope is offline reward labeling, batch RLHF, and quality-sensitive alignment settings where per-query Information Processing and Management 63 (2026) 104957 20 S. Chen and Y. Liu inference of several seconds at the 8B scale can be batched; real-time production use such as content moderation or sub-second filtering would require distillation or architectural simplification. The limitations suggest five future directions: (i) more efficient architectures via mixture-of-depths or sparse high-risk-step verification; (ii) step-level feedback during policy training for intermediate reward shaping; (iii) extension to multi-modal settings (code execution, visual reasoning, scientific experiments); (iv) human-in-the-loop active learning over the interpretable step-level outputs; and (v) tighter sample complexity bounds for specific task classes and certified robustness under stronger adversarial models.

A.2. Robustness against reward hacking Reward hacking, where a policy exploits reward model weaknesses to receive high rewards for low-quality outputs ( Gao et al. , 2023 ; Skalse et al. , 2022 ), is a central failure mode. The analysis below decomposes adversarial success into the joint event that every step-level verifier fails simultaneously.

sections.heading: A.3
sections.text: ( Conditionally Independent Step Failures ) . Conditioned on the internal reasoning trace 𝑅 internal , verification failures at distinct steps  𝑘 are conditionally independent. This is an idealized assumption: correlated failures, such as a shared reasoning error that propagates across steps, reduce the effective number of independent checks and weaken the bound. In practice, Tier 2 can still inspect whether an error in step 𝑘 propagates to later steps because Tier 1 reasoning is generated before step-level verification.

sections.heading: A.4
sections.text: ( Gaussian Verification Noise ) . Adversarial perturbations to input responses contribute zero-mean Gaussian noise with variance 𝜎 2 to each step’s verification margin. For a per-token verification strength 𝛼 step > 0 , this gives the tail bound P (  𝑘 ) ≤ exp(− 𝛼 step 𝐷 ∕ 𝜎 2 ) . Non-Gaussian noise would change the tail form but not the qualitative monotonicity in 𝐾 and 𝐷 when the per-step tail probability decreases with depth.

Define the reward hacking event as  hack = { HPR 𝜃 ( 𝑥, 𝑦 bad ) > HPR 𝜃 ( 𝑥, 𝑦 good )} , where 𝑦 good is a high-quality response and 𝑦 bad is a low-quality response designed to exploit the model. Then under Assumptions A.3 – A.4 : P (  hack ) ≤ exp ( − 𝛼 ⋅ 𝐾 ⋅ 𝐷 𝜎 2 ) , (A.12) where 𝛼> 0 is a verification strength parameter that increases with the granularity of process-level verification. In this idealized model, an adversarial response must simultaneously fool all 𝐾 verification checkpoints, each conditioned on 𝐷 tokens of context. This formalizes the design intuition, motivated by shallow alignment findings ( Qi et al. , 2024 ), that verification should be distributed throughout the reasoning process. The analysis below states the marginal-benefit condition for an optimal allocation under a fixed expected token budget.

A note on curriculum reinforcement learning

sections.heading: A.4
sections.text: ( Convergence of Curriculum Reinforcement Learning ) . A formal convergence proof for the three-phase curriculum RL (step-level → trajectory-level → preference-level) would require extending existing multi-objective RL convergence theory ( Ouyang et al. , 2022 ) to hierarchical, non-stationary reward functions. We leave this as an open theoretical question and note that empirically, training loss converges monotonically within 6 epochs across all experiments ( Fig. 7 ). The decreasing KL penalties across phases ( 𝛽 step > 𝛽 traj > 𝛽 pref ) are motivated by the intuition that coarser objectives require less exploration once fine-grained verification has been established.
